articles.title: Why a fresh wave of North Korean soldiers may fight in Russia's war in Ukraine
articles.summary: North Korea will continue to send its soldiers to fight in Russia's war, but only for as long as it is profitable to do so, writes the BBC's Quentin Sommerville.
articles.body:
An enemy that swarmed the battlefield in large groups while under fire, seemingly oblivious to the dangers of drones and fire from automatic weapons. An elite corps of ghost soldiers who chose suicide over surrender. They fought and died in their thousands, then apparently vanished from the battlefield.

North Korea's soldiers were sent to fight by Pyongyang alongside Russian forces as they sought to repel a Ukrainian offensive on Moscow's territory at the end of 2024. They paid a heavy price, as many as 3,000 killed in action from the 13,000 deployed.

Ultimately, they would adapt their tactics, and with Russia would drive Ukrainian forces from its Kursk region. In combat terms, little has been heard of them since, but according to Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, North Korean forces, and their weaponry, are soon to make a dramatic return to Russia's war in Ukraine.

Last month, Zelensky warned that up to 50,000 North Koreans will be deployed in Russia, revising an earlier estimate of 30,000 troops. He called on South Korea to provide support for his country's air defence.

But why, after such heavy losses, would North Korea send more men to fight for Russia, and what happened to its soldiers sent in the first place?

"They're still there", said Dr Yang Uk, research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, Center for Foreign Policy and National Security in Seoul. "They are defending Russian territory for another counterattack from Ukraine. And we believe that some of the engineer corps or workers might be in [the Russian-occupied] Donbas area but that's not the combat troops."

The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, HUR, estimates that 8,500 North Korean servicemen are still on Russian territory. They are organised into four brigades, which operate as part of the "North" Group of Forces and are assigned to protecting the state border of the Russian Federation in the Kursk Region from Ukrainian incursions.

"They do not participate in active combat operations. Units of the Korean People's Army have not been observed in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," HUR said in a statement to the BBC.

For North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un, the Kursk deployment was a gamble, its largest combat force ever sent overseas. (In 1973, North Korea sent 1,500 military personnel and instructors to Egypt during the Yom Kippur war with Israel, and in the late 1960s, an estimated 87 North Korean pilots fought for the North Vietnamese against US forces).

And despite the bloodshed, it was a gamble that paid off, reaping countless benefits for the isolated and impoverished country, transforming both its economic and military fortunes. And one that could serve as a blueprint for even deeper military cooperation.

North Koreans, "now know what modern combat is about", said Yang.

The soldiers sent to fight in Russia were from Storm Corps, the elite of the North Korean armed forces. Extremely isolated, totalitarian North Korea is a militarised and heavily indoctrinated state.

At first, neither Russia, nor North Korea, even acknowledged their presence. Ukrainian forces first clashed with them in November 2024, and the first live North Korean prisoners of war wouldn't be captured until January of the following year.

It wasn't until April 2025 that Russia first acknowledged their role, when Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, described their "heroism" on the battlefield.

Yang continued, "North Korean soldiers are very brave I mean, especially those of Storm Corps. They are willing to die for their country. But the problem is that passion doesn't mean efficient combat skills... [They suffered] a lot of bloodshed in the early stage of the Kursk campaign, but they learned the lessons of modern drone warfare."

"Cannon fodder", is how "Sultan", a soldier with Ukraine's 95th Air Assault Brigade described North Korean troops. He faced them in the battle for Kursk at the end of 2024.

"They would begin with one large assault group, then another 15–20 men would be sent into the same position, and then more after that. The North Koreans operated differently. They kept moving all the time. That gave them a certain advantage, but not a decisive one," he recalled recently in Kyiv.

Communication between them and their Russian allies appeared poor, he said, and their soldiers were inadequately equipped.

After combat, Sultan and his men would search enemy corpses for documents and intelligence information. On the Russian dead they would find personal belongings, identification and equipment. "But when we searched the North Koreans specifically, the only thing we found on them was simply ammo. We checked absolutely all the small pockets - there were no documents, nothing at all," he explained.

Other Ukrainian soldiers reported the North Koreans lacked body armour, winter clothing and helmets.

In one chilling video from a Ukrainian assault, a wounded North Korean soldier lies prone on the snow-covered ground in a wooded area. As the Ukrainians approach, he detonates a grenade under his chin, after calling out, with his last words, the name of his leader, Kim Jong Un.

In April 2025, at a memorial service in Pyongyang at the newly created Museum of Foreign Military Operations, Kim praised heroes who choose suicide over capture.

In a speech to relatives, with Russia's Defence Minister Andrey Belousov in attendance, he said they were "heroes who unhesitatingly opted for self-blasting, suicide attack, in order to defend the great honour".

While North Korea has never officially acknowledged the death toll from the Kursk operation, a BBC Korea analysis of the memorial site estimated that 2,300 soldiers were killed fighting for Russia.

Ukraine's intelligence arm, HUR, puts the figure at 3,000 killed and 1,500 injured.

But aside from the combat experience, why did North Korea sacrifice so many of its best troops in a foreign war?

The deployment has been a much-needed economic windfall for the country and a geopolitical win, according to Lim Soo-ho, a senior research fellow at the Institute for National Security Strategy, in Seoul.

He estimates that arms sales to Russia and the troop deployment have netted the impoverished country close to $10bn.

"North Korea's annual GDP is estimated at around $30bn (£22bn)," he told me. "That means they earned a third of a year's GDP over two and a half years through weapons exports and troop deployment, which, for an economy as small as North Korea's, is a very significant effect."

In exchange for its manpower, North Korea gets food, oil and hard currency. While China says it complies with sanctions against Pyongyang, Russia does not.

But equally important, the cooperation with Russia has shifted North Korea's long-term dependency on China.

So in Beijing in September last year, Kim Jong Un was able to stand shoulder to shoulder with China's leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in the first public meeting of all three. Not quite as an equal, but no longer reliant on China alone.

This is significant, said Lim, "It's a major geopolitical shift".

"Whenever things got difficult under isolation, North Korea would reach out first toward South Korea, Japan, or especially the US to try to normalise relations, that was the pattern of Korean Peninsula diplomacy. But now that ties with Russia have tightened, Kim Jong Un argues that the world is in a new Cold War, a multipolar system."

The arrangement with Russia, which began as economic and military expediency appears to be developing into something deeper and longer-term. At this year's 9th Party Congress of the Korean Workers' Party, Kim Jong Un was emboldened and spoke of accomplishments that his grandfather Kim Il Sung and father Kim Jong Il never achieved.

But dangers lie ahead. To date, no North Koreans have fought on Ukrainian or Russian-occupied Ukrainian land. If they did so, there would be diplomatic consequences, not least in South Korea, an ally of Ukraine, albeit one which so far has only provided "non-lethal" aid.

This is something that President Zelensky has emphasised as he presses for Seoul to provide advanced military hardware, including air defence systems. He said that since June, preparations have been underway in Russia's Voronezh region to receive fresh North Korean forces and claimed that Pyongyang was preparing to transfer additional ballistic weapons to Russia.

"Russia is helping North Korea learn modern warfare, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience. This poses a threat to every country in Asia that lies within range of North Korean missiles," he said in a presidential address in July.

Only two North Korean soldiers were captured alive in battles with Ukrainian forces. That's a staggeringly low number, given that between 11,000 and 14,000 fought in the Kursk campaign. (Another was captured alive but died from combat-related injuries, according to the South Korean National Intelligence Service).

Like their comrades who choose suicide over capture, neither man intended to be taken alive.

"For Joseon (North Korean) soldiers, becoming a prisoner of war itself is a crime. That just isn't an option. We can't become POWs," one of the captured men told a South Korean MBC documentary crew who interviewed him in prison in Ukraine.

Baek Pyeong-gang, not his real name, lay wounded from a drone strike for four days before being captured. He was tricked into surrendering when he mistook Ukrainian soldiers for his Russian allies.

The second prisoner, Lee Kang-eun, also a pseudonym, told the journalist Kim Young-mi that he felt guilty he was still alive. Barely conscious, he was found by Ukrainian soldiers on the battlefield with extensive injuries to the arm and jaw.

"I had no grenade or knives on me to self-blast (end my life)," he explained.

He described scores of his colleagues killed by drones, early in the war. The battlefield "reeked of the smell of blood", he said.

Neither man wants to return to North Korea, Lee said he believed that his family members would be "wiped out" as punishment for his capture. Both have said they want to be sent to South Korea, and Seoul is willing to take them.

Only Russia, not Pyongyang, has asked for their return.

But Ukraine, still intent on pressuring Seoul for military aid, has not committed to handing them over to South Korean authorities. Kyiv has said it will honour international human rights obligations which prevent the forced repatriation of prisoners of war.

Their fate remains undecided, but what appears certain is that more North Koreans will join Russia's war. Their service has enormous economic and political value to Pyongyang; but Russia desperately needs them too.

Four and a half years into Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it is facing a desperate manpower shortage. Western and Ukrainian intelligence agencies estimate that it is losing some 6,000 more troops a month than it can recruit. So, Moscow has been forced to turn to foreign fighters, from Colombia, Kenya, Cameroon and North Korea, to sustain its ranks.

For Russia and North Korea, it is a mutually beneficial relationship, a coalition at a price. Ultimately, North Korea will continue to send its soldiers to fight in Russia's war, but only for as long as it is profitable to do so.

articles.body:
Cooperativa consolidou sua posição entre as maiores instituições financeiras do Brasil ao alcançar o 7º lugar no ranking dos 100 maiores bancos do Valor 1000 de 2026, refletindo seu crescimento sustentável e a força do modelo cooperativo. — Foto: Sicredi

O Sicredi foi destaque na edição 2026 do Valor 1000, anuário organizado pelo jornal Valor Econômico que reúne as maiores empresas do país. Na categoria “100 Maiores Bancos”, a instituição financeira cooperativa conquistou a 7ª posição, mantendo o destaque alcançado nas edições mais recentes do ranking.

O reconhecimento acompanha uma trajetória consistente de crescimento do Sicredi. Em julho de 2026, a instituição superou a marca de R$ 500 bilhões em ativos totais. Hoje, está presente em mais de 2,1 mil municípios brasileiros, com mais de 3,1 mil agências e uma base de 10,5 milhões de associados.

O Prêmio Valor 1000, tradicional iniciativa do Valor Econômico, reconhece anualmente empresas de destaque em diferentes setores da economia brasileira. A premiação integra o anuário Valor 1000 e considera diversos indicadores para avaliar o desempenho e a posição das companhias em seus respectivos segmentos. Ao longo dos anos, consolidou-se como uma das principais referências do cenário empresarial brasileiro.

articles.title: Segurança da Virgínia: quem era o tenente e pastor morto em Goiás | G1
articles.standfirst: Rogério Camilo Ramos e sua esposa, Paulla Regina, morreram em um acidente de moto na BR-060 neste domingo (13). O casal, que também atuava como pastor.
articles.summary: O segurança da Virgínia, Rogério Camilo Ramos, e sua esposa Paulla Regina morreram em um acidente de moto na BR-060, em Goiás, gerando comoção entre familiares e amigos.
articles.body:
Rogério Camilo Ramos e Paulla Regina Rodarte Camilo — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Rogério Camilo Ramos, de 51 anos, que morreu em um acidente de moto com a esposa, Paulla Regina Rodarte Camilo , era tenente da reserva, pastor de uma igreja evangélica e segurança particular da influenciadora Virgínia Fonseca. Rogério e Paulla morreram na manhã deste domingo (13), na BR-060, na região do Ribeirão da Posse, em Guapó , na Região Metropolitana de Goiânia . Eles receberam homenagens da igreja onde exerciam o ministério e também da polícia.

Em nota, a Fundação Tiradentes lamentou a morte de Rogério Camilo e Paulla Regina. A instituição disse que ele era 2º tenente e veterano da Polícia Militar (PM). A nota de pesar deixa sentimentos para os familiares e amigos do casal e deseja que a memória deles permaneça viva através do respeito e da saudade.

"Neste momento de profunda dor, expressamos nossos mais sinceros sentimentos aos familiares e amigos. Que Deus conforte os corações de todos e conceda força para enfrentar esta irreparável perda", diz o comunicado.

A fundação informou que o velório e o sepultamento de Rogério e Paulla vão acontecer no Complexo Vale do Cerrado, na rodovia GO-060, entre Goiânia e Trindade, com datas e horários ainda a serem definidos.

Rogério e a esposa também eram pastores da igreja evangélica Viver é Cristo, em Goiânia. No perfil oficial, a igreja informou que o culto deste domingo (13) foi cancelado e publicou uma nota de pesar dedicada aos líderes religiosos do local.

"É com o coração entristecido que nos solidarizamos com a família, amigos e toda a igreja pela partida do nosso querido Pr. Rogério Camilo e Prª. Paulla Rodarte", diz trecho da publicação.

Paulla Rodart e Rogério Camilo — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram Paulla e Rogério

Rogério Camilo também trabalhava como segurança particular da influenciadora Virgínia Fonseca. Ela lamentou o acidente e disse que ele era seu segurança. Segundo Virgínia, Camilo estava com ela em São Paulo há pouco tempo, onde ajudou com a segurança das crianças. Ela disse estar em choque e sem entender. Em uma postagem no Instagram, a influenciadora lamentou a morte do casal.

"Minha ficha ainda não caiu. Camilo estava com a gente agora em SP, sempre prestativo, me ajudando com a segurança das crianças, e hoje sofreu um acidente com a esposa e partiram. Eu estou em choque, coração partido e sem entender o porquê, mas ninguém explica os planos de Deus", escreveu Virgínia.

Virgínia postou uma homenagem ao segurança Camilo — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram Virgínia

De acordo com a Rota Verde Goiás, o acidente aconteceu no quilômetro 201 da rodovia, no sentido sul, na região do Ribeirão da Posse, em Guapó, na Região Metropolitana de Goiânia. Segundo a concessionária, Rogério Camilo e Paulla Regina estavam em uma motocicleta. A morte do segurança, que conduzia o veículo, foi confirmada pela médica da Rota Verde às 9h02.

Paulla Regina era passageira, foi encontrada em parada cardiorrespiratória e recebeu atendimento com o apoio do Corpo de Bombeiros, mas não resistiu e teve a morte confirmada às 9h26, informou a Rota Verde.

A concessionária da via disse ainda que a causa do acidente só será determinada pela perícia depois de análise e investigação. De acordo com a empresa que administra o trecho, a rodovia está devidamente sinalizada. A Rota Verde Goiás lamentou profundamente o ocorrido e manifestou solidariedade aos familiares e amigos das vítimas

articles.summary: US Streamers News: A surprise encounter with Kim Kardashian left Candace Owens scrambling for a moment before Kanye West’s Chicago concert. Owens recently described seei.
articles.body: A surprise encounter with Kim Kardashian left Candace Owens scrambling for a moment before Kanye West’s Chicago concert. Owens recently described seeing Kardashian across a lobby while she was speaking with someone from Kanye’s team. The unexpected sighting brought an awkward pause, especially given Owens’ past public comments about Kardashian. Still, the moment ended without confrontation, and Owens later said there were no hard feelings.Candace Owens describes tense Kim Kardashian encounterCandace Owens opened up about the unexpected meeting on her podcast, recalling the moment she looked across the lobby and noticed Kim Kardashian. She said her immediate reaction was essentially an oh-s*** moment.The situation was made more uncomfortable by the history between the two women. Owens acknowledged that she had made public comments about Kardashian over the years, making the possibility of spending the evening in the same area feel particularly awkward.For a brief moment, the two reportedly looked at one another from opposite sides of the lobby. Owens compared the exchange to the kind of silent tension captured by a viral meme. Despite the uncomfortable start, however, the encounter did not turn into an argument or public confrontation.That detail appears to have been important to Owens. Rather than describing the meeting as hostile, she portrayed it as an awkward celebrity run-in that simply caught both women off guard.Kim Kardashian was in Chicago for North WestOwens later learned that Kardashian was not actually attending Kanye West’s concert. She was in Chicago because of her daughter North West’s performance the following night.That discovery quickly changed the situation for Owens. What initially looked like a potentially long and uncomfortable evening suddenly became far less concerning.Owens also made clear that she did not view the encounter as the start of a new feud. She said there were "no hard feelings" and sent love to Kardashian and her family.The concert itself eventually became the main attraction for Owens. She said she left the box and moved into the crowd because the atmosphere was simply too energetic to stay seated.Adding another memorable detail, Owens joked about being eight months pregnant while still feeling ready to crowd surf. The comment gave the story a lighter ending after what had initially been an unexpectedly tense moment.For all the speculation that can surround celebrity encounters, this one ultimately ended quietly. Two people with a complicated public history crossed paths, exchanged a look, and moved on. articles.title: Europe beats US 15-13 in Solheim Cup. Lowry takes Irish Open by record 11 shots
articles.summary: The Solheim Cup is back in the hands of the Europeans after they won seven of the 12 singles matches Sunday at Bernardus for a 15-13 victory over the United...
articles.body:
DEN BOSCH, Netherlands (AP) — The Solheim Cup is back in the hands of the Europeans after they won seven of the 12 singles matches Sunday at Bernardus for a 15-13 victory over the United States.

The blue wave came early and never really went away, with Lottie Woad holing a putt from 2 feet on No. 17 to guarantee Europe reaching the 14 1/2 points needed to beat the United States. Moments later, Carlota Ciganda closed out her match over Jennifer Kupcho for the final point.

Ciganda also won the point that retained the Solheim Cup for Europe in 2023.

The Europeans have now won three of the last five editions, the only loss in that stretch coming in Virginia two years ago.

The teams were tied at 8-8 after two days and set out Sunday in heavy rain for the singles, with Europe going out fast and putting blue all over the scoreboard. Early wins for Charley Hull and Linn Grant set the tone. The only wobble coming when U.S. player Alison Lee came from 4 down after 11 holes to beat Esther Henseleit, 1 up, for the biggest comeback in Solheim Cup history.

Europe now has won the last three times on home soil.

DOONBEG, Ireland (AP) — Shane Lowry gave his home crowd and President Donald Trump plenty to cheer Sunday when he turned a four-shot lead into a runaway at Doonbeg, closing with a 7-under 63 to break the Irish Open record with an 11-shot victory.

Lowry opened with four birdies in eight holes, one of them from 45 feet over a ridge at No. 7, and the Irishman poured it on before a delirious gallery at Trump International Ireland.

He finished on 23-under 257, seven shots better than the previous 72-hole record of 264 by Jon Rahm at Lahinch in 2019. Lowry won by 11 shots over Patrick Reed (64) and Joaquin Niemann (67), breaking the Irish Open record by one shot for the largest victory margin. Bernhard Langer held the record of 10 shots at Portmarnock in 1987.

Lowry won the Irish Open for the second time, 17 years after he won as an amateur.

SIOUX FALLS, S.D. (AP) — Zach Johnson won the Sanford International on Sunday for the fifth victory of his first PGA Tour Champions season, birdieing the final two holes to edge Ben Crane by a stroke.

The 50-year-old Johnson closed with a 4-under 66 at Minnehaha Country Club to finish at 11 under. He matched Stewart Cink for the tour victory lead.

Crane also shot 66. He finished birdie-birdie-bogey-birdie.

Mario Tiziani had a 63 to tie for third at 8 under with Boo Weekley (64), Ryan Armour (66), Chad Campbell (67) and 2025 winner Retief Goosen (68).

Johnson won 12 times on the PGA Tour, highlighted by major titles at the 2007 Masters and 2015 British Open.

FRANKLIN, Tenn. (AP) — Alvaro Ortiz of Mexico won the Simmons Bank Open on Sunday for his second Korn Ferry Tour title of the year, closing with a 7-under 63 for a four-stroke victory.

The 30-year-old Ortiz finished at a tournament-record 26-under 254 at Vanderbilt Legends Club. He opened with rounds of 65, 61 and 65.

Ortiz also won the UNC Health Championship in a playoff in May in Raleigh, North Carolina.

Sandy Scott of Scotland was second after a 67.

Etienne Papineau of Canada won the PGA Tour Americas' Digital Commerce Group Open at Uplands Golf Club in Victoria, British Columbia. He finished with a 9-under 61 to reach 25-under 255. Charlie Nikitas was four strokes back in second. ... Kosuke Sunagawa closed with a 3-under 69 for a two-shot victory in the Shinhan Donghae Open for his first Japan Golf Tour title ... Former LIV Golf player Frederik Kjetterup shot 5-under 67 and held on for a one-shot victory in the English Trophy to claim his first Challenge Tour title. ... Samuel Simpson closed with a 5-under 65 for a one-shot victory in the SunBet Challenge on the Sunshine Tour in South Africa. ... Miyu Yamashita, the 2025 Women's British Open champion, closed with a 3-under 69 and defeated Yuzuki Yoshizawa in a playoff to win the Sony JLPGA Championship. ... Bokyeom Park won the KB Financial Group Golden Life Championship by closing with a 1-under 71 to win by one shot on the Korea LPGA.

articles.title: Missing 70-year-old hiker rescued after disappearing for a week in remote national park
articles.summary: A Coast Guard helicopter crew hoisted Craig Berg to safety after he went missing for a week while hiking in Michigan’s remote Isle Royale National Park.
articles.body: A 70-year-old man who vanished a week ago while hiking in Isle Royale National Park was found "alive and alert" Saturday, according to officials. Craig Berg was suffering from hypothermia when he was rescued by Coast Guard and Michigan State Police crews, officials said. "The Coast Guard and Michigan State Police rescued an injured, ailing man Saturday after he went missing in Isle Royale National Park on Sept. 5," the U.S. Coast Guard Great Lakes said. Video released by authorities shows a helicopter crew from Coast Guard Air Station Traverse City hoisting Berg from the ground. He was then taken to a regional airport in Gwinn for emergency medical evaluation. MISSOURI DEPUTY AG, MISSING 6 DAYS AFTER SEEKING TO SUMMIT WYOMING'S TALLEST PEAK, IS FOUND ALIVE Officials did not disclose what happened to Berg while he was missing or provide additional details about his injuries. Berg was spotted by "good Samaritan" backpackers in the park Saturday before Michigan State Police foot patrols and K-9 units reached him, according to officials. Multiple agencies and resources were deployed to aid the emergency search, which also included a 45-foot Coast Guard boat, drones and seaplanes. The search involved the National Park Service, Michigan Department of Natural Resources, Keweenaw County Sheriff’s Office, Wisconsin State Patrol and Minnesota Department of Public Safety, according to Lt. Ben Eckola, a Michigan State Police public information officer. "We’re also thankful to the fellow hikers who helped, Isle Royale Seaplanes, and No One Left Behind K9 Search and Rescue. Everyone’s efforts played an important part in finding Craig," Eckola said in a statement. ILLINOIS MAN MISSING MORE THAN A WEEK AS CREWS SCOUR GREAT SMOKY MOUNTAINS NATIONAL PARK The Detroit Free Press reported that Berg, of Royal Oak, Michigan, arrived at the national park on Aug. 27 for an extended solo hike but failed to return home Sept. 5. Isle Royale National Park is located on a remote island in Lake Superior near the Canadian border. Due to its remote location, Isle Royale is one of the least-visited national parks and has limited infrastructure. Berg’s wife, Debbie, told the Detroit Free Press that only two rangers are stationed on the island and that the park has two camp stores and a lodge. articles.title: Charlie Kirk statue vandalised outside Turning Point USA headquarters
articles.summary: Vandals spray red paint on Charlie Kirk statue days after its unveiling to mark one year since his death.
articles.body:
A new memorial statue of the slain right-wing activist Charlie Kirk has been vandalised days after it was installed outside Turning Point USA’s headquarters, the youth-focused organisation he co-founded.

Turning Point chief operating officer Tyler Bowyer said on Sunday that the bronze statue, alongside an accompanying sign, was defaced with red spray paint in Phoenix, Arizona.

“This morning we woke up to radical criminals vandalizing our Headquarters. Crossing over Charlie’s face, scratching out Jesus and the Cross & spraying red paint on his neck,” Bowyer wrote on X.

The statue was unveiled on Thursday to mark one year since Kirk’s death. Kirk, a co-founder of Turning Point and staunch ally of US President Donald Trump, was fatally shot while speaking to students at Utah Valley University.

The man accused of killing Kirk, Tyler Robinson, faces a possible death penalty after pleading not guilty to murder charges earlier this month.

Phoenix police said they received calls on Sunday morning about a vandalised memorial outside Turning Point’s headquarters.

Turning Point accused the vandals of intentionally spraying the statue’s neck, the spot where Kirk was shot in the attack , which was captured on video.

“We will restore the statue and replace the signs, but we are also reviewing the footage of the incident and are working with law enforcement to identify who did this and hold them accountable,” Turning Point said in a post on X.

articles.title: Amazon suspends use of 21 Air, cargo carrier involved in fatal Miami crash
articles.summary: Online retailer Amazon said Sunday it was suspending its use of cargo carrier 21 Air after one of its Amazon-branded aircraft crashed upon landing in Miami this month, killing five people.
articles.body: Online retailer Amazon said Sunday it was suspending its use of cargo carrier 21 Air after one of its Amazon-branded aircraft crashed upon landing in Miami this month, killing five people. Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel did not divulge specific factors but said the decision came after the company reviewed some of the circumstances around the crash as it supported the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation into its cause. “After the tragic incident last weekend, we’ve spent time supporting the investigation and reviewing some of the surrounding circumstances, and we’ve decided to pause our operations with 21 Air, the operator of Flight 7598,” Nantel said. Amazon has said it will use other carriers to transport shipments that would have been assigned to 21 Air. Its other carriers include Sun Country Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, Air Transport International, ABX Air, ASL Airlines and Cargojet. North Carolina-incorporated 21 Air, which specializes in cargo shipments to and from Mexico, said in a statement Sunday that it remains focused on supported those affected by the crash “as well as working closely with the NTSB and all our partners, like Amazon, as the investigation continues.” “We are confident in our safety policies, procedures and training,” 21 Air said. In the hours after the crash, 21 Air CEO Keith Winters offered condolences to the families of the dead and injured and cooperation to investigators. “Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives,” he said in a statement. “Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the authorities, and ensuring that accurate information is communicated as it becomes available.” Five people were killed and five were injured when a 21 Air Boeing 767-300 overran a runway at Miami International Airport just before 2 p.m. ET Sept. 6 while it was landing, according to officials. It struck two vehicles, including a van carrying workers for an airline cleaning service. All five people who were killed were on the ground; authorities identified them as Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47. Flight 7598 was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, when it overran Runway 30 and struck two vehicles before it stopped, Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said. Data from the flight’s cockpit voice recorder (CVR) revealed that as one pilot was trying to land, the other cautioned repeatedly that the aircraft was going too fast, but there was no “consistent verbal response to the comments about speed,” according to a summary of the CVR data released by the NTSB. The data suggested that the plane touched down, and about 15 seconds later a pilot called for a go-around, a maneuver in which a plane aborts its landing by pulling up and circling around to try to land again. The NTSB’s investigator in charge of the probe, Chihoon Shin, said the aircraft’s flight data recorder showed its thrust increased during landing in a way that was consistent with a go-around attempt. He also said, “The speed brakes and the thrust reversers were not deployed.” Speed brakes are active flaps commonly deployed to help an aircraft slow down, while thrust reversers are often used to help slow a plane upon landing. Shin said it was not clear why they might not have been deployed. The investigation into the crash continues. Nantel of Amazon said, “We’ll continue working to support the investigation and everyone affected.”

articles.title: US aviator shot down over Iran recalls 'free-falling' in first interview
articles.summary: The April rescue operation to recover the downed aircrew saw the first US boots on the ground in Iran in 46 years, American officials say.
articles.body:
A US Air Force officer has described "free-falling" to the ground with a damaged parachute after his plane was shot down over Iran, leading to a dangerous rescue operation.

"At one point when I looked up and saw no parachute, that was the most terrifying thing I've ever seen," said the aviator, who was not named in the interview with CBS News' 60 Minutes programme.

The segment, which aired on Sunday, is the first time one of the aviators involved in the April incident over Iran has spoken out about their ordeal.

The two US troops ejected from the damaged plane, were separated, and had to evade Iranian forces while they awaited rescue from US special forces.

"Free-falling is a good way to put it," said the US airman, who was identified by the name Bravo during the CBS segment.

"I wasn't focused on the speed at which I was falling. I was instead focused on trying to correct the problems that were in front of me and doing anything I could to unfurl or pull pieces of the parachute loose," he said.

He called his survival "a miracle", although he broke his back, shoulder and arm. The speed at which he hit the ground was "somewhere between 70 and 100mph (113 to 161km/h)".

The other US airman who was shot down, identified as Alpha, declined to be interviewed by CBS.

How rescue of US airman in remote part of Iran unfolded

The $30m two-seat F-15E jet was taken down by a shoulder-fired missile, which costs around $100,000, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner network.

Bravo said that despite his injuries, he hiked and climbed to the top of a tall ridgeline, in fear of Iranian forces the whole way.

"Never let a lack of motivation put you on Iranian TV," he said.

Alpha was rescued within six hours, in an operation that involved intense fighting, said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.

"It was a gun fight all the way in and all the way out," Hegseth said. "But they got Alpha back."

Bravo was rescued after 48 hours behind enemy lines.

At one point there were over 90 US service members on the ground inside Iran, said Central Command Admiral Brad Cooper, noting that it was the first time in 46 years that American forces were operating inside Iran.

But planes and helicopters needed to evacuate became stuck in the desert sand and needed to be destroyed while special forces awaited a backup rescue crew.

Two of the destroyed US aircraft were worth about $100m each, CBS says, noting that several "Little Bird" helicopters also needed to be destroyed so the technology would not be obtained by Iran.

The operation came about five weeks into the war against Iran, which was launched by the US and Israel.

Now in its seventh month, the war has become increasingly unpopular among the US public as it heads into campaigning season ahead of the congressional midterm elections in November.

Much of this dissatisfaction stems from a steep rise in global energy prices and the knock-on effects on other goods.

Last week, US President Donald Trump predicted that the war would continue until at least election day on 3 November.

articles.title: Jaxson Dart takes brutal hit early in Giants vs Cowboys opener but what happened next was kind of surprising
articles.summary: Jaxson Dart took a brutal hit from DeMarvion Overshown along the sideline, but the Giants QB avoided the blue medical tent despite his concussion history.
articles.body: Jaxson Dart got absolutely rocked in the first quarter of Sunday night's regular-season opener between the New York Giants and Dallas Cowboys. It happened along the Giants sideline. Indeed, it happened on the white (out of bounds) area along the Giants sideline. And then some interesting things happened: Dart went flying into some equipment along that sideline and immediately raised up to make sure everyone understood he was fine. His teammates, obviously not appreciating that Cowboys linebacker DeMarvion Overshown knocked their starting quarterback into hard sideline stuff while he was clearly out of bounds, went after the linebacker. A MASSIVE BRAWL AT COWBOYS AND SAINTS JOINT PRACTICE INCLUDES PUNCHES AND HELMETS THROWN AND WWE MOVES Then Cowboys players rallied to defend Overshown. And we had beef among the opposing players, NFL style. You know, guys pushing and shoving while wearing helmets and more padding than an ancient gladiator. NEW NFL FINE SCHEDULE IS GOING TO A POINT SYSTEM THAT COULD LEAD TO SUSPENSIONS BUT ALSO REFUNDS Officials stepped in a restored order by throwing a flag on Overshown and the Cowboys for unnecessary roughness. That cost the Cowboys 15 yards above the 22 yards Dart had already gained on his run. But here's the intrigue: Dart didn't get summoned into the blue medical tent. He clearly took a significant hit that could have easily caused the Unaffiliated Neurotrauma Consultant to force Dart into the tent. But it didn't happen. And, you may recall, that's something Dart lobbied for in a manner of speaking during the preseason. Dart expressed frustration after being summoned to the Giants’ blue medical tent during an Aug. 9 preseason game against the Vikings, saying he respected the NFL’s safety rules but was "puzzled" he always seemed to wind up in the tent every time he was hit. Dart said he believed the hit in that particular game had merely knocked the wind out of him. He was cleared to return after the evaluation. But the QB wasn't happy about having to leave the game. His history, by the way, explains the heightened scrutiny. During his 2025 rookie season, Dart was sent for concussion evaluations five times and was diagnosed with one concussion. That caused him to miss two games. He also exited a November game against the Bears after suffering that concussion, although he returned later in the season and finished the year. Sunday night's hit was no less aggressive and severe as any of the ones Dart endured last year. But, again, no trip to the tent. So here's a conspiracy theory: SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS Maybe Dart helped himself by complaining in August. No one is saying independent doctors would fail to do their jobs in protecting vulnerable players. But perhaps Dart earned himself the benefit of the doubt. articles.title: Creepy 'Cat in the Hat' trend targets schools as costumed figure allegedly chases teen girl
articles.summary: A person dressed as the Cat in the Hat allegedly chased a teen girl in British Columbia as the creepy trend sparks school threats nationwide.
articles.body: A shadowy figure dressed as the Cat in the Hat allegedly chased a teenage girl through a Canadian neighborhood, as a creepy online trend featuring sinister depictions of the beloved children’s character has prompted investigations and school warnings targeting schools and students across multiple states. The unidentified girl was walking in West Kelowna, British Columbia, at about 9 p.m. Aug. 24 when a person wearing a costume resembling the Dr. Seuss character allegedly began chasing her, according to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The teen escaped and reached her home safely, but police are still working to identify the costumed individual. POLICE IDENTIFY SUSPECT ACCUSED OF TERRORIZING PHILADELPHIA WOMEN WHILE WEARING CREEPY CHUCKY-STYLE MASK "Regardless of whether the individual intended the behavior as a joke, following a young person and causing them to fear for their safety is extremely concerning," Cpl. Devon Gerrits said. "People should understand that behavior intended as a prank can have serious consequences when it causes another person to reasonably fear for their safety." TIMELINE REVEALS HOW MAN IN 'CHUCKY' MASK TERRORIZED PHILADELPHIA STREETS, EVADED POLICE Investigators said wearing a costume is not a crime by itself, but pursuing someone in a way that causes reasonable fear could constitute criminal harassment. Assault, threats or intimidation charges could also be considered depending on the evidence. Anyone who believes they are being followed or pursued should move toward a populated location, contact a trusted adult and call 911 if they are in immediate danger, the West Kelowna RCMP advised. Police are asking anyone with doorbell, security or dashcam video taken near the 2000 block of Shamrock Drive at about 9 p.m. Aug. 24 to contact the West Kelowna RCMP. Police have not said whether the real-world chase is connected to a separate "Cat in the Hat" social media trend that has spread across the United States, putting schools on alert and landing some juveniles in custody. LOUDOUN COUNTY TRANSGENDER SUBSTITUTE CHARGED WITH MAKING SCHOOL THREATS The online trend features edited or AI-generated images and videos depicting a sinister version of the Cat in the Hat lurking outside homes, standing near schools or prowling through communities. Some anonymous accounts have added the names of students, staff members, campuses and towns, sometimes accompanied by ominous messages or threats. Authorities from California to Florida, Virginia and Texas have responded with investigations and increased patrols as they work to separate internet hoaxes from credible dangers. TIKTOK IN LEGAL HOT SEAT AS STATE ACCUSES APP OF EXPOSING KIDS TO HARMFUL CONTENT WHILE MISLEADING PARENTS The Baldwin Park Police Department in California said it was reviewing "concerning social media posts" that referenced local schools and named students and staff members. "Any threat directed toward our schools, students, staff, or community will not be dismissed as a joke or prank," the department warned. NEW MEXICO SEEKS MASSIVE PENALTY FROM META AFTER JURY FOUND TECH GIANT LIABLE FOR ENDANGERING CHILDREN Police urged residents not to interact with or recirculate the accounts. Anyone who encounters a threatening post is asked to preserve the content, account name, screenshots, dates and times before reporting it to investigators. In Virginia, the Hanover County Sheriff’s Office launched an investigation after an account posted content referencing Mechanicsville High School and the trend. Deputies increased their presence at the campus while attempting to identify the person behind the account. UK TO BAN TIKTOK, YOUTUBE, OTHER SOCIAL MEDIA APPS FOR CHILDREN UNDER 16, STARMER SAYS The sheriff’s office similarly urged residents not to repost the material, warning that doing so could amplify the message and complicate efforts to trace its origin. Florida’s St. Johns County Sheriff’s Office said it was investigating content involving county schools but had not identified a credible threat. Deputies nevertheless increased their presence on campuses across the county as a precaution. Texas law enforcement agencies have also warned that creating or spreading the threatening posts could carry consequences far beyond school discipline. The Frio County Sheriff’s Office said some anonymous accounts have attached lists of students, schools or communities to menacing images and videos in an apparent attempt to provoke fear. Authorities there determined posts mentioning the area did not appear to present a credible threat but increased patrols and law enforcement visibility around schools. "Participating in, re-creating, or spreading these threatening posts is not a harmless joke," the sheriff’s office said, warning that copycat accounts and forwarded threats could lead to charges involving cyberbullying, harassment or terroristic threats. Laredo police delivered a similar warning, saying criminal charges and arrests may follow even when the person responsible claims the post was only meant as a prank. GIRL OBSESSED WITH SANDY HOOK, COLUMBINE ALLEGEDLY PLOTTED SCHOOL MASSACRE WITH OTHER STUDENTS: REPORT "A few seconds on social media can result in a police investigation, school disciplinary action, and potentially serious criminal consequences," the department said. Premont police met with school district leaders after learning of the trend and warned that fake accounts, AI-generated content and purported pranks involving threats could result in charges including making a terroristic threat or filing a false alarm or report under Texas law. The warnings come as authorities in multiple states have traced threatening accounts to juveniles. Four girls between 13 and 15 years old were arrested in Berwick, Louisiana, after police linked them to TikTok accounts that alarmed families and schools, according to Police1. Three were charged with terrorizing or menacing, while a fourth was charged with cyberbullying. A 12-year-old Florida student was accused of posting a written threat to kill tied to the trend, while a 14-year-old Colorado student was arrested after a post referenced a middle school and several homes, the outlet reported. Authorities in Alabama, Ohio and Kentucky have also announced juvenile arrests or pending charges connected to similar posts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Police across the affected communities have repeatedly asked parents and students not to share the content, even when attempting to warn others. Instead, users should capture screenshots showing the account name and threatening material and send the evidence directly to school officials or law enforcement. Fox News Digital reached out to TikTok for comment.

articles.title: Air Force officer recalls ‘free-falling’ after jet was shot down over Iran
articles.summary: In an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes,” one of the two U.S. Air Force officers whose fighter jet was shot down over Iran in April detailed his harrowing ordeal.
articles.body: In an interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday, one of the two U.S. Air Force officers whose fighter jet was shot down over Iran in April detailed his harrowing ordeal, including plummeting to the ground with a damaged parachute. The Defense Department has not identified the Air Force colonel by name. “60 Minutes” correspondent Norah O’Donnell said the show agreed to refer to the weapons systems officer by his mission call sign, “Bravo,” because of security threats from the Iranian regime. In the interview, the lead segment on the 59th season premiere of the CBS newsmagazine, Bravo said he felt like he had been “hit by a freight train” when a shoulder-fired missile rammed into his F-15E two-seat fighter jet on April 2. The other Air Force officer hit the eject button. “I will be thankful to my dying day for my pilot and crewmate, Alpha, for saving our lives and ejecting us,” Bravo told O’Donnell. Bravo said he started “free-falling” toward a rugged mountainous area. He looked up and saw that his parachute had been damaged in the missile attack — a realization he called “the most terrifying thing I’ve ever seen.” Military professionals estimate he hit the Iranian desert somewhere between 70 and 100 mph, he said, adding that his survival was a “modern-day miracle.” “60 Minutes” reported that the fall broke Bravo’s back, arm and shoulder, yet he managed to hike and climb a 7,000-foot ridgeline to evade capture. He was stranded behind enemy lines for two days without food or water before two elite Air Force pararescue operators got him out of harm’s way. “Let’s go,” Bravo said he told his rescuers. “60 Minutes” characterized the search-and-rescue operation as one of the most complex and risky in U.S. military history. (Sunday’s segment did not feature an interview with Alpha, who landed 5 miles away from Bravo after they ejected from the F-15E.) “60 Minutes” returned to the airwaves Sunday after a summer of turmoil at America’s leading broadcast newsmagazine. CBS News Editor in Chief Bari Weiss undertook a sweeping shake-up at the show in late May. She tapped technology journalist and documentarian Nick Bilton as the program’s new executive producer, cut ties with a group of senior leaders and let go of two correspondents, Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi. Scott Pelley, a veteran correspondent, excoriated Bilton at a June 1 staff meeting, questioning his qualifications for his role and objecting to the ousters of Vega and Alfonsi. Pelley was fired the next day. Alfonsi had previously clashed with Weiss over a segment about the Trump administration’s deportation of Venezuelan men to a prison in El Salvador. Weiss and Bilton have since hired new on-air talent, including Ross Douthat, a former opinion columnist at The New York Times who is now a “60 Minutes” correspondent, and Sebastian Junger, a reporter and author who became a contributor to the series. Bilton announced in late July that O’Donnell had been elevated to full-time correspondent. Sunday’s season premiere offered a glimpse of the revamped program, with slight adjustments to its on-air graphics. The two other segments that aired Sunday were an investigation into “brokers” paid to seek pardons from the Trump administration and an inside look at the Los Angeles Rams football franchise. In the episode’s final minute, Douthat said “60 Minutes” was planning stories about the artificial intelligence boom. “We may have a narrow window — this year, not the next 10 — to make artificial intelligence safe for humanity. That clock is ticking, and so is ours,” Douthat said, accompanied by the show’s signature “tick-tick-tick” sound effect. “For almost 60 years, it has meant the same thing: journalism you can trust. Where we’re headed, we’re going to need it.”

articles.title: Philippines’ Muslim-majority Bangsamoro region votes for first parliament
articles.summary: However, deadly violence marred the elections one day before the polls open in the southern Philippine region.
articles.body:
Nearly 2.4 million voters in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in the southern Philippines are casting their ballots in the first parliamentary elections since the region was established in 2019.

Monday’s historic vote is seen as a crucial step towards self-governance after decades of insurgency and violence in the Muslim-majority region.

There are 80 seats up for grabs in the elections that will determine members of parliament, the region’s legislative body. These include 40 political party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives.

The region’s chief minister, who heads the executive branch, will be elected by parliament in its first session.

Election officials said they were targeting a turnout of at least 80 percent after polling was postponed for several years.

However, deadly violence marred the elections one day before the polls opened.

The chairman of the Commission on Elections, George Garcia, reported on Monday that Cotabato City had been put under the commission’s control after a shooting late on Sunday killed three people and injured 15 others. In separate incidents in the city, he said a blast from an improvised bomb injured the person carrying the explosive, and a gun was fired but no one was hurt.

The town of Maluso in Basilan was also put under the commission’s control after pre-shaded ballots were found in 36 out of 68 precincts. Garcia said he ordered the immediate reprinting of ballots for the affected precincts where voting would be delayed.

Garcia vowed to charge those who attempt to sow violence or buy votes.

“These elections stand on generations of Bangsamoro struggle for homeland, identity, and self-determination, in the face of dispossession, marginalization, conflict and sacrifice,” he said in an earlier statement.

Polling stations are due to close at 7pm local time (11:00 GMT).

The election marks the end of the transition period under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA), an interim regional government appointed in 2019.

Established under a 2014 peace deal , the BARMM aims for broader autonomy, with former Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) rebels agreeing to demobilise and giving up their goal of a separate Muslim state in the south of the largely Catholic country.

Since the 1970s, about 150,000 people have died in the conflict. The area was once a haven for extremist groups but has seen a decline in violence.

Abdullah Macapaar, centre, along with some of the fiercest Muslim rebel commanders in the southern Philippines, takes his oath during a ceremony for the creation of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) at the Presidential Palace in Manila, Philippines, on February 22, 2019 [Bullit Marquez/AP]

articles.title: Amazon crash: Firm pauses work with cargo carrier after fatal incident
articles.summary: The 21 Air-operated jet overshot a runway at Miami International Airport and hit several vehicles.
articles.body:
E-commerce giant Amazon says it is suspending work with the firm that operated a cargo plane that was involved in a fatal crash in Miami this month .

"After the tragic incident last weekend, we've spent time supporting the investigation and reviewing some of the surrounding circumstances, and we've decided to pause our operations with 21 Air," an Amazon spokesperson said on Sunday.

On 6 September, the 21 Air-operated Boeing jet overshot a runway at Miami International Airport and hit several vehicles, killing five people.

The BBC has contacted 21 Air for comment. The firm previously said it was "devastated by the accident" and that it is cooperating with authorities to investigate the incident.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is leading the investigation into the crash.

Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said: "Safety has always been our top priority, whether in our own operations or when we're working with partners."

"We'll continue working to support the investigation and everyone affected," she added.

21 Air is an all-cargo carrier that operates flights for major firms like Amazon and DHL.

The Boeing 767-300 cargo plane crashed in Miami after departing from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

The aircraft overshot the runway, crashing into nearby vehicles before skidding to a stop.

Last week, Miami authorities identified the five people who died as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.

"Our deepest condolences are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives," 21 Air chief executive Keith Winters previously said.

"Our immediate priorities are supporting those affected, assisting the appropriate authorities, and ensuring that accurate and verified information is communicated as it becomes available," he added.

NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy called the crash site a scene of "utter devastation".

The safety board's investigators have recovered the flight recorders to analyse the conditions leading up to the crash.

Investigators released details that a pilot onboard the cargo plane noted that it was going too fast before it overshot the runway, the NTSB said in the early stages of investigation.

It said that one of the pilots warned the other pilot multiple times about "the aircraft's excessive speed" but noted "there was not a consistent verbal response", even as an altitude alarm sounded.

There were other electronic warnings designed to alert the pilots to danger while landing, investigators reported.

articles.title: Niger mutiny exposes growing reliance on Russia
articles.summary: The attempted power grab has exposed deep grievances within the army and tested Niger’s ties with its Sahelian allies.
articles.body:
Niamey, Niger – The failed mutiny in Niger has shown the extent to which President Abdourahamane Tiani now relies on Russian support when his government comes under threat, including from within his own security forces.

On August 29, soldiers calling themselves the Armed Forces for the Restoration of the Homeland attacked Air Base 101 at Niamey’s international airport, the presidential palace and the national broadcaster in a coordinated assault. A statement circulated during the fighting falsely declared that Tchiani had been removed.

Loyalist presidential guard units held the palace overnight, while about 200 Russian Africa Corps soldiers, backed by drones and reportedly reinforced from Mali and Libya, helped retake the airbase by evening. At least 27 people were killed, and about 100 mutineers were arrested.

The mutiny showed who Tchiani could rely on when his own security forces turned against him. Nigerien troops held the presidential palace, while Russian personnel and equipment helped loyalist forces retake the key airbase.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Ryan Cummings, head analyst at Signal Risk, said the attempted mutiny was rooted in grievances that had been building inside the military.

“The insurrection indicates discord within the Nigerien armed forces,” he said. “This stems from multiple sources. The foremost pertains to significant casualties being inflicted against the country’s military by an array of non-state armed actors which appear to be as well equipped, if not better, than their military counterparts.”

Cummings pointed to a widening gap between soldiers fighting on the front lines and those protecting the country’s political leadership.

“Other factors include discrepancies in deployment and remuneration between low- to middle-ranking officers, who led the attempted mutiny and putsch, versus their more senior counterparts, such as the presidential guard who thwarted the coup attempt,” he said.

“Junior to middle-ranking soldiers are generally deployed to conflict front lines, where they face well-equipped and increasingly professional militant units that are capable of overrunning their positions,” Cummings noted. “Conversely, more senior military units, most notably the presidential guard, are deployed to garrisoned cities such as Niamey and Agadez, where the threat of engagement is generally lower. Despite facing a lower risk profile, senior military units generally enjoy significantly higher remuneration than their low- to middle-rank counterparts.”

The mutiny exposed the gap between soldiers fighting on the front lines and those serving in better-protected units in the capital.

Tchiani expelled French and American troops in 2023 and 2024, and troops from Russia’s Africa Corps entered Niger as the military government sought to replace Western support.

But the mutiny showed that Moscow’s role now goes beyond helping Niger fight armed groups.

When soldiers inside Niger’s own military threatened the government, Russian personnel and equipment helped loyalist forces retake Air Base 101. The episode showed that Russia’s role in Niger now extends beyond the fight against armed groups to helping protect the military government itself.

That is a significant shift from how the partnership was initially presented to Nigeriens: as a way to strengthen the fight against armed groups after the departure of Western forces.

For Tchiani, that reliance on Moscow comes as he faces continued attacks by armed groups and growing discontent among soldiers fighting them.

The response from Niger’s fellow military leaders also raised questions about how much help the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) can provide when one of its members is under serious pressure.

According to Romane Dideberg, a research analyst at Chatham House’s Africa Programme, the response was one of the most revealing aspects of the rebellion.

“What the security response says about the cohesion of the Alliance of Sahel States might be one of the most telling elements of the mutiny,” she said. “As with the April attacks in Mali, the two other Sahelian juntas remained largely unreactive during this existential moment for the Nigerien junta, reacting only once the mutiny was neutralised.”

“This partly reflects the operational shortcomings of the confederation’s security architecture, but also, more critically, the sensitive relations between Tchiani’s junta and his Malian and Burkinabe counterparts,” she said.

Dideberg said Tchiani was rumoured not to have reached out to Mali. She also pointed to a generational and cultural gap between Tchiani and his Sahelian allies, saying his government showed more continuity with the former establishment while a different rationale had underpinned the coup that brought him to power.

The mutiny tested how far the three miltary governments were prepared, and able, to come to one another’s aid.

Alongside the Russian role, allegations have emerged that French and Emirati interests were connected to the mutiny, amid wider friction over Niger’s Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline project.

The allegations have not been independently substantiated.

Roger Gabriel, a Nigerien army captain and commander of the elite 1st Parachute Battalion, appeared on state television on September 4 and alleged that several people, including associates of deposed President Mohamed Bazoum and officers from Chad, Benin and the Ivory Coast, were behind the attack.

He also said people from the United Arab Emirates had called and urged him to join the mutiny.

The claims are difficult to independently verify, but they have put fresh attention on the UAE’s growing presence in the Sahel.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an Africa analyst at the Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the possibility of Emirati involvement “cannot be dismissed” given the information circulating and the UAE’s broader regional activity.

“The UAE has been expanding its influence across the Sahel, from the western states to Sudan, primarily through official partnerships with military regimes, but also via informal networks, resource extraction, notably gold, and ties to non-state actors including separatist groups when needed,” he said.

“Its approach is pragmatic and dual-track: it prioritises formal state-level relations first, then pivots to alternative channels if the official path falters,” Ibrahim said.

“All of this is deeply political and strategic, interlinked with ambitions to secure leverage over Mediterranean and Red Sea routes. The growing friction with Algeria underscores how these moves are widely read in the region as an effort to reshape the balance of influence, making any allegations around the recent events in Niger worth careful scrutiny rather than either exaggeration or dismissal,” he said.

For now, the allegations remain allegations.

Tchiani survived the mutiny, but the failed attempt to remove him exposed strains inside his military, highlighted his growing reliance on Russia, and raised questions about how much help his closest regional allies can provide when he needs it.

For Dideberg, the implications go beyond the failed attempt to unseat Tchiani.

“This mutiny calls the effectiveness, but also, to an extent, the sincerity, of the mutual assistance pact into question,” she said.

articles.title: Air Force colonel shot down over Iran reveals desperate prayer in 50-hour fight to survive
articles.summary: An Air Force colonel survived a 70-100 mph parachute fall into Iran with three broken bones and evaded enemy capture for 50 harrowing hours.
articles.body: An Air Force colonel shot down over Iran survived a terrifying fall, three broken bones and a two-day enemy manhunt after turning to God as his damaged parachute sent him plunging toward the desert. The colonel, identified only by his mission call sign "Bravo," revealed in a new interview with CBS News’ "60 Minutes" how a desperate prayer began an extraordinary 50-hour fight to make it home alive. "At one point when I looked up and saw no parachute, that was the most terrifying thing I’ve ever seen," Bravo said in his first public account of the April ordeal. "So I paused, right then, and I prayed, ‘Lord, your will be done. But if I’m getting through this, I need help.’" HOLLYWOOD LEGEND MAKING MOVIE ABOUT EPIC IRAN RESCUE MISSION TO SAVE F-15 FIGHTER JET CREW The colonel was the weapons systems officer seated behind the pilot of an F-15E Strike Eagle operating under the call sign Dude 44 when an Iranian shoulder-fired missile struck the aircraft April 2, according to CBS News. OPERATION EPIC FURY SHATTERED IRAN’S POWER, BUT EXPOSED RISKS AMERICA CAN’T IGNORE The two-man crew had been assigned to attack industrial facilities tied to Iran’s drone and missile program near a mountainous region south of Isfahan, U.S. Central Command leader Adm. Brad Cooper told the outlet. "We had air superiority, but clearly we weren’t flying over Kansas," Cooper said. THE LEGACY OF 'EAGLE CLAW': HOW FAILURE HELPED BUILD AMERICA'S ELITE SPECIAL FORCES Bravo described the missile strike as feeling like the jet had been hit by a freight train. He and the pilot, known as "Alpha," initially tried to save the roughly $30 million aircraft before realizing they had no choice but to eject. Alpha escaped safely, but the missile had damaged Bravo’s parachute, sending him hurtling toward the ground at an estimated 70 to 100 mph, CBS reported. SEAL TEAM 6 MEMBER REVEALS EPIC DETAILS OF OSAMA BIN LADEN RAID The violent landing broke Bravo’s back, arm and shoulder and left him stranded roughly five miles from Alpha in the heart of enemy territory. Despite his injuries, Bravo moved away from his landing site and began climbing toward a roughly 7,000-foot ridgeline as daylight revealed the desert valley and steep cliffs surrounding him. SEAL TEAM 6 MEMBER EXPLAINS BLUNT REALITY OF COMBAT AND EXPECTATIONS IN THE BLACK OPS WORLD "Never let a lack of motivation put you on Iranian TV," he told CBS. Iranian forces were actively hunting the downed aviators and at one point came within several hundred meters of Bravo, according to U.S. military officials cited by the outlet. Images of the wrecked American fighter jet had already appeared in Iranian media, while videos reportedly showed armed groups searching the region. PETE HEGSETH HEADS TO CAPITOL HILL TO DEFEND TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS 60-DAY CONGRESSIONAL DEADLINE LOOMS "There was clear intent out of the Iranian ground force to come find those two guys," Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine told CBS. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said he was awakened in the middle of the night and informed that the fighter jet had been shot down. "Whether they’re alive or not, we’re going to go get them," Hegseth recalled. American forces rescued Alpha about six hours after the crash during a dangerous daylight mission in which U.S. helicopters came under fire. "It was a gun fight all the way in and all the way out," Hegseth said. "But they got Alpha back." Bravo, however, could not be found. TRUMP OPENS HORMUZ UNDER FIRE WITH ‘PROJECT FREEDOM’ AS IRAN WARNS OF ATTACKS In a statement provided to "60 Minutes," Alpha praised the combat search-and-rescue teams and other U.S. forces involved in bringing both men home. "Words cannot capture how thankful my family and I are and how proud I am to serve alongside each and every one of them," Alpha said. The pilot has since returned to flying but declined to appear publicly because of security concerns, CBS reported. As darkness fell on Bravo’s first day in Iran, the injured colonel managed to send a message to U.S. forces. "God is good," he wrote. Bravo also told commanders that he was injured but still moving. Military leaders considered launching another rescue operation that night, but Hegseth said the conditions did not come together and officials made the agonizing decision to leave the colonel in Iran for another day. Bravo endured the high desert’s wind and cold with almost no food or water while American forces tracked both him and the Iranian teams trying to capture him. The CIA launched a deception campaign designed to confuse Iranian forces and used classified technology to pinpoint Bravo’s location, according to CBS. Newly declassified footage showed U.S. bombers and drones striking nearby forces linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as the rescue mission moved into place. More than 90 U.S. service members entered Iran on the ground, marking the first American boots inside the country in 46 years, Cooper told the outlet. Hundreds more took part in the air, while thousands provided support. Two large search-and-rescue aircraft landed on a makeshift desert runway before smaller "Little Bird" helicopters flew toward Bravo’s position on the ridgeline. Bravo called the moment he saw his rescuers "one of the greatest moments of my life." His first words to them were simple: "Let’s go." But the dangerous operation was not over. TRUMP SAYS US WILL 'BEAT THE F------ S--- OUT OF THEM' AFTER IRAN LAUNCHES SURPRISE MISSILE STRIKE The landing gear of the two rescue planes became trapped in the desert sand, stranding Bravo and more than 90 elite U.S. service members. A clandestine Air Force unit was ultimately brought in to extract the group, CBS reported. The U.S. military then destroyed the two stranded aircraft, each valued at roughly $100 million, along with the smaller helicopters to prevent sensitive American technology from falling into Iranian hands. Bravo was finally safe about 50 hours after Dude 44 was shot down, with the rescue completed as the sun rose on Easter Sunday. The colonel, who called his survival a "modern-day miracle," said he believes God carried him through the fall and the harrowing days that followed. "I believe that it’s a testament to God’s provision in my life to bring me through that moment in a way that didn’t prevent injuries, but prevented any catastrophic injuries that would have affected my ability to survive," he told CBS. Bravo said his ordeal was ultimately bigger than one downed aviator. Bravo's first public account aired during the season premiere of CBS News' "60 Minutes," marking the start of the program's first season under editor-in-chief Bari Weiss and executive producer Nick Bilton.

articles.title: California football coach arrested after students make disturbing discovery at school
articles.summary: The Tracy Unified School District placed the educator and football coach, Jeffrey Pribble, on leave as separate criminal and district investigations continue.
articles.body: A high school football coach in California was arrested Friday after students discovered a cellphone secretly recording them while they were changing inside a campus locker room, police said. The phone belonged to Jeffrey Pribble, a 48-year-old teacher at Tracy High School, located east of San Francisco, the Tracy Police Department said Saturday. According to the school's website and social media accounts, Pribble is the varsity football head coach and works in the school's physical education program. Pribble has held the coaching position for five years and has 22 years of experience as an educator with the district, according to his Facebook page. SCHOOL EMPLOYEE ACCUSED OF SECRETLY FILMING 12 GIRLS IN CHANGING ROOM FACES NEW CHARGES The discovery was made Thursday when a student and several classmates found the phone recording inside the locker room, officials said. The students stopped the recording, deleted the video and turned the device over to a teacher. By Thursday evening, a concerned parent then contacted Tracy police patrol officers, prompting school resource officers and detectives to open an investigation. The following day, officers determined that the phone belonged to Pribble, who was arrested Friday. The Tracy Unified School District placed Pribble on leave pending the outcome of separate criminal and district investigations, officials said. According to the Pleasanton Weekly, Tracy High Principal Jon Waggle acknowledged the arrest of an employee in an email to parents. FLORIDA MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHER ADMITS TO YEARS OF 'INAPPROPRIATE' CONVERSATIONS WITH FORMER STUDENT: DEPUTIES The school did not identify the teacher or the specific allegations but noted that the district was fully cooperating with police. "We understand that this news may raise serious concerns in the District community. The District too is concerned about the well-being of its students and staff and is committed to holding its employees to the highest professional and ethical standards," Waggle wrote. "Tracy High School and all our Tracy Unified schools are proud of being safe schools. The cooperation between students, parents and staff members keeps our schools safe and is important and appreciated. Thank you for your continued partnership and support." Tracy Police Chief Sekou Millington added that the safety and privacy of the city's students remain among the department's top priorities. "Our children deserve to feel safe at school and in every space where they should be able to learn, grow, and simply be kids," Millington said. We are grateful to the students who brought this incident to the attention of adults and to the officers and detectives who acted quickly to investigate." articles.title: Giants honor 9/11 heroes before emotional Sunday Night Football opener against Cowboys
articles.summary: MetLife Stadium's 9/11 tribute before Giants vs. Dallas Cowboys featured the Tribute in Light, FDNY's Ladder 343 truck and a giant American flag.
articles.body: Before the Giants took to the field against the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday Night Football, MetLife Stadium marked the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks with a pregame tribute honoring victims and first responders. Fans arriving at MetLife Stadium were welcomed by FDNY’s ceremonial Ladder 343 truck and an authentic World Trade Center steel beam displayed outside the gates by the Tunnel to Towers Foundation. Two vertical columns of light, echoing the World Trade Center’s "Tribute in Light," illuminated the night sky above MetLife Stadium. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The ceremony included a special performance of the national anthem by members of the NYPD and FDNY. On the field, players, coaches and Giants season-ticket members held a 100-yard wide American flag stretching from end zone to end zone. New York City first responders formed a gauntlet for the Giants during player introductions. Players, coaches and staff from both teams wore commemorative NYPD, FDNY and PAPD hats on the sideline, while players and coaches wore "Never Forget" T-shirts during warm-ups. NFL'S WEEK 1 9/11 TRIBUTE BEGINS IN SEATTLE WITH WILD GUITAR SOLO DURING NATIONAL ANTHEM Members of the Palumbo family, whose FDNY father died on 9/11, served as honorary captains for the coin toss. A photo montage of lives lost on 9/11 played on the stadium’s video boards during a moment of silence. Giants legends also joined uniformed first responders for the "Go Big Blue" chant before kickoff. SON WHO LOST FATHER IN 9/11 ATTACKS SHARES POWERFUL LESSONS 25 YEARS LATER: ‘I’M STILL HERE’ For new Giants coach John Harbaugh, who took over after 18 seasons in Baltimore, the tribute carried special significance. "It’s a story about heroes who were willing to run toward danger while others were trying to escape it," Harbaugh said. "To be in New York and honor the heroes of that day who live on forever in our culture, that means everything. You honor it with your effort." articles.title: Japanese PM-backed candidate wins Okinawa gubernatorial election
articles.summary: Genta Koja beat two-term incumbent Denny Tamaki, who wants a major US military base to be moved out of Okinawa.
articles.body:
Genta Koja has defeated two-term incumbent Denny Tamaki in the race for governor of Japan’s southernmost prefecture, potentially ending more than a decade of opposition to a United States military build-up in the region.

He won 59 percent of the vote in Sunday’s election, officials announced on Monday.

Koja, a former deputy mayor of Okinawa’s capital, Naha, was backed by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party. He beat Tamaki, 66, who has long pushed for a major US military base to be moved out of Okinawa.

The 42-year-old will become the youngest Okinawa governor since the prefecture was returned to Japan from US rule in 1972. He will also become its first governor born after the reversion.

His election could end Okinawa’s legal efforts to block the relocation of US Marines from the Futenma air base to a new facility at Henoko on the prefecture’s main island, according to Masaaki Gabe, a professor emeritus at the University of the Ryukyus.

Gabe also said it may make it easier to expand military access to airports and ports.

“Koja could reasonably be expected to approve their designation, opening wholly civilian facilities to military use,” Gabe added.

Koja’s victory comes as Takaichi prepares to unveil a new national security strategy this year that is expected to accelerate Japan’s biggest military build-up since World War II.

Her administration said increased defence spending was necessary to deter China from using military force to advance its territorial ambitions in East Asia.

Okinawa forms part of what military planners call the first island chain, a string of territory stretching from Japan through the Philippines that constrains China’s access to the western Pacific.

Yonaguni Island, Japan’s westernmost territory, lies 110km (68 miles) east of Taiwan. Beijing claims Taiwan as its own territory and has stepped up military activity around the democratically governed island.

Tensions between Tokyo and Beijing have risen since Takaichi said last year that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could also threaten Japan and trigger a military response by Tokyo.
